stops.name: Belfast, birth in College Square East
stops.campa: William Thomson is born in a house in College Square East, hard by the Royal Belfast Academical Institution where his father James teaches mathematics and engineering to the sons of the linen merchants. He is the fourth of seven children, a delicate boy in a house ruled by figures and diagrams. James Thomson, self-made out of an Ulster farm, has resolved that his sons will not merely learn mathematics but live inside it, and the discipline of that resolve will outlast the father by seventy years, carried first to Glasgow and then round the whole compassed earth by cable and calculation.

stops.name: Belfast, the death of Margaret Gardner Thomson
stops.campa: William's mother, Margaret Gardner, dies when he is six years old, leaving James Thomson alone with seven children and the whole of their upbringing. The father does not remarry; he takes the education of William and his elder brother James wholly into his own hands, tutoring them at his own table with a rigor that will mark both boys for life. The household becomes a small academy of two pupils and one exacting master, its curriculum mathematics, its discipline unbroken attention, and its only holiday the annual family excursion to the Continent to see waterfalls, glaciers, and instruments.

stops.name: Glasgow, the family removes to the College
stops.campa: James Thomson is elected Professor of Mathematics at the University of Glasgow, and the whole household migrates from Belfast to the college on the High Street, then still a cluster of medieval-looking courts before the move west to Gilmorehill. The two eldest boys, James and William, are entered as students of their own father's university at an age when other children are still in the nursery. The College becomes literally their home: they live within its walls, attend its logic and Greek and mathematics classes, and grow up thinking of a university as a family's ordinary furniture.

stops.name: Glasgow, matriculation at the University, aged ten
stops.campa: At ten years old William is formally entered on the matriculation roll of the University of Glasgow, sitting in classes of young men twice his age. He wins prizes in Latin, Greek, astronomy, and natural philosophy through his teens, but it is the mathematics and the physical sciences that hold him: he reads far beyond the set texts, borrowing what the college library and his father's shelves can supply. Already the family jokes that he thinks in equations the way other boys think in games, and that a blackboard is his native element.

stops.name: Glasgow, the Essay on the Figure of the Earth
stops.campa: In the astronomy class of session 1839-40, fifteen-year-old William submits an essay on the figure of the Earth so mathematically accomplished that the professor, doubting a boy could have written it unaided, at first withholds the prize. It is finally awarded, a gold medal, and the essay's methods, on the mechanics of rotating, self-gravitating bodies, will occupy Thomson's mind on and off for the rest of his career, a problem he returns to in moments of personal difficulty as another man might return to prayer or verse.

stops.name: Glasgow, reading Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur
stops.campa: At the end of the session William reads Jean-Baptiste Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur and is transformed by it: a mathematics of heat flow built on differential equations of a beauty he has met nowhere else. British mathematicians of the older school, suspicious of Fourier's series, are still attacking the book; the sixteen-year-old writes and publishes, under the signature 'P.Q.R.', his first papers in its defence. The taste for continental analysis fixed in him this summer, married to heat and to Carnot's engines, will in eight years yield the absolute scale that bears his later name.

stops.name: Cambridge, matriculation at Peterhouse
stops.campa: William enters Peterhouse, the oldest and smallest of the Cambridge colleges, in the Michaelmas term of 1841. He has come already reading Fourier and Laplace, so far ahead of the Tripos syllabus that his private coach must slow him down rather than push him on. He rows, plays whist, edits and writes for the newly founded Cambridge Mathematical Journal, and keeps up, through it all, an unbroken correspondence with his father in Glasgow, who tracks every examination and every friendship with the same close attention he once gave the boy's Latin.

stops.name: Cambridge, the Colquhoun Sculls
stops.campa: William wins the Colquhoun Sculls, the university's premier single-boat race on the Cam, one of the few undergraduates of his year to combine first-rank mathematics with a rowing man's physique and nerve. He keeps a scull, a French horn, and a stack of mathematical journals in the same rooms, and friends of this period remember him as tirelessly sociable rather than the popular caricature of the isolated genius: he organizes concerts, edits a journal, and trains on the river before returning to work through the night on unsolved problems in electricity and heat.

stops.name: Cambridge, the founding of the University Musical Society
stops.campa: Among the undergraduates who found the Cambridge University Musical Society, William gives his evenings to concerts and part-singing with the same appetite he gives his mornings to Green's and Fourier's mathematics. He plays the French horn indifferently but with enthusiasm, and will keep a taste for music, and later for the sea, as the two disciplines outside mathematics that never leave him. Classmates already sense in him something unusual: a mind that treats a symphony, a scull-race, and a partial differential equation as parts of one continuous pleasure.

stops.name: Cambridge, Second Wrangler and the Smith's Prize
stops.campa: Through twelve days of written examination in the Senate House, William is placed Second Wrangler, behind Stephen Parkinson of St John's, a result his friends and later historians alike call an accident of the Tripos's peculiar scoring rather than a true measure of the two men. A week later the university corrects itself: in the Smith's Prize examination, judged by different examiners on deeper mathematical ground, Thomson is placed unambiguously first. Within months he is elected a Fellow of Peterhouse, the college's youngest in memory.

stops.name: Cambridge, the recovery of George Green's forgotten Essay
stops.campa: Preparing to leave for Paris, William hears a chance mention of an obscure 1828 pamphlet by the miller-mathematician George Green, dead four years and almost unknown. No copy can be found in the Cambridge booksellers or the college libraries; at last a fellow of Caius produces one from his own shelves. Reading it, Thomson recognizes at once a theory of potential far ahead of its time, buried by Green's total obscurity. He carries the little book to Paris in his luggage, determined that Liouville and the French mathematicians will not let it die a second time.

stops.name: Paris, the laboratory of Henri Victor Regnault
stops.campa: Thomson spends the autumn of 1845 working in the laboratory of Henri Victor Regnault at the Collège de France, the most exact experimental physicist in Europe, whose measurements of the properties of steam and gases underlie every steam engine's design. Here the Cambridge mathematician, until now a creature of pure analysis, learns for the first time the discipline of the instrument bench: the endless patience of calibration, the distrust of any number not independently checked. It is Regnault's painstaking data on gases that Thomson will use, three years later, to calculate an absolute scale of temperature founded on theory rather than on the accident of mercury or water.
